items.summary: Grep to confirm old references are gone before claiming a fix is done
items.details: During the first PR #470 pass, the status.md rough-edge section was reported as updated for the fmt.Printf reference. Copilot caught that the update was incomplete — the section heading still mentioned fmt.Printf, line 83, and the confidence table still said 'fmt.Printf in hot path'. The lesson: after editing a doc to fix a stale reference, grep for the old text to verify it is gone. 'I updated it' is not the same as 'the old text no longer appears'.

items.summary: Do not put exact line numbers in long-lived docs
items.details: status.md and quality.md both referenced 'handler.go:695' for the PlayerDisconnected TODO. The actual line is 691. Line numbers shift with every refactor, making the reference wrong within days. Copilot caught this and suggested removing the line-specific reference entirely. The fix: describe the location by symbol or context ('in the stream-disconnect path of handler.go') rather than by line number, unless you also commit to updating the reference on every refactor.

items.summary: Verify cross-repo relative links — they only resolve in a workspace mono-repo
items.details: status.md had a link '../../rpg-project/CLAUDE.md' which resolves correctly in a workspace where both repos are siblings under ~/personal/, but fails on GitHub where rpg-api is a standalone repo with no ../rpg-project neighbor. The fix is to use an absolute GitHub URL (https://github.com/KirkDiggler/rpg-project/blob/main/CLAUDE.md) for cross-repo references, or link to the repo's own CLAUDE.md for the subset of the content that is local.

items.summary: Read actual code before describing its behavior — do not infer from context
items.details: The event processor rough-edge entry claimed 'fmt.Printf to log publish failures'. The code actually uses _, _ = p.publisher.Publish(...) — errors are silently discarded, no logging at all. This is arguably worse than fmt.Printf. The error originated from describing the behavior without reading the file. The fix: always read the target file and cite the specific pattern. 'Verified by reading X:Y' beats any inference.

items.summary: Enforce coord-space contracts at the producer / merge boundary, not at consumers
items.details:
Issue #493 was the sixth bug of the same shape: a piece of cumulative encounter state emitted in room-local coordinates when the rest of the cumulative state had been translated to dungeon-absolute. Specifically, RoomLayout.walls in EncounterStateData.rooms were untranslated while EntityState.position and RoomData.CubeEntities were absolute. The visual symptom (rooms overlapping in the client) and the gameplay symptom (cross-room targeting / pathing failures) both trace back to this single producer.

Lessons: (1) When you have two coordinate spaces, declare ONE canonical frame for cumulative state and enforce it at every producer that writes to that state. (2) Do not put translation in consumers — it spreads the discipline across an unbounded surface area, and any new consumer that forgets to translate becomes a bug. (3) When you find one producer is the wrong frame, grep for sibling producers in the same data structure (here: rooms[] map fields, entities[] map fields, CubeEntities) before assuming you've fixed it. (4) Cube invariant X+Y+Z=0 is preserved under origin addition because both LocalPosition and AbsolutePosition satisfy it independently — no special-case math needed at the merge site.

Applying this discipline closes the runtime data-flow bug class. Type-level unification (one Position type, one numeric width) is a separate discipline tracked as #465 and is what would prevent these bugs from being writeable in the first place.

items.summary: Loaders for cross-room state must iterate every revealed room, not just CurrentRoomID
items.details:
Issue #465's wall-consumer scope was the seventh bug of the cross-room class. After #493 fixed the cumulative producer (encounterStateData.rooms[].walls translated to absolute), Kirk's playtest showed two remaining symptoms: (1) outer perimeter walls of the revealed room not rendering, and (2) characters could not path INTO the revealed room from room A. Both traced to the SAME shape — different sites — namely loaders that filtered to dungeon.GetRoom(currentRoomID).Walls and treated that as the encounter wall set.

Four wall-consumer call sites had this pattern: MoveCharacter, executeMoveAction, executeMonsterTurns, ResolveAttack. Each one independently loaded only currentRoom.Walls. The fix was a single helper loadAbsoluteWallsForRevealedRooms that iterates dng.RevealedRooms and translates each room's walls to dungeon-absolute. All four sites now call the helper.

Lessons: (1) Producers AND loaders are both subject to the cross-room discipline. The producer/consumer distinction (lesson-coord-space-discipline) was about coord-space; the loader scope is about WHICH rooms are in the working set. Both must agree with the cumulative-state contract. (2) When you fix one bug at a producer and the symptom only partially resolves, grep for siblings in the OPPOSITE direction (consumers / loaders that read the same kind of data). The bug was producer-side AND loader-side; fixing only the producer left half the surface broken. (3) The wall validator's frame-agnostic property (pure 2D segment intersection) is what makes the absolute-frame rewrite safe — same code works on local and absolute as long as both inputs agree. Without that property, the fix would have required a per-room iteration that stayed in each room's frame.

Door passability falls out for free: the perimeter generator splits walls AROUND the door hex (createWallBeforeDoor / createWallAfterDoor), so the door is a gap in the wall list. No special-case logic in the collision check; just don't break the wall list with a producer or loader that does it wrong.

Applying this closes the wall-consumer scope of #465. Type-level unification (the other scope of #465) remains separate.
